screens.title: Introduction to AWS Global Infrastructure and Edge Locations
screens.narratorSegment: Today we begin with the physical foundation that underpins cloud reliability and speed. You will learn what Regions, Availability Zones, and Edge Locations are, why AWS separates them, and how that separation helps you design resilient, low-latency systems. Think of Regions as independent geographic clusters, Availability Zones as separate data centers inside a Region that share an AWS backbone, and Edge Locations as compact points of presence placed close to users for fast content delivery. We will also cover the two-tiered caching strategy used by CloudFront — local Points of Presence and larger Regional Edge Caches — plus how services like Global Accelerator and WAF use edge infrastructure to improve performance and security. By the end of this chapter you'll know which infrastructure component to choose for static assets, dynamic compute, or latency-sensitive traffic, and you'll be able to spot a common mistake: treating edge services as optional rather than strategic. As we move forward, think about your users’ geography and the nature of your content — those two facts drive the best architecture choices.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Intro to AWS Global Infrastructure
Introduction to AWS Global Infrastructure and Edge Locations
Understand the roles of Regions, Availability Zones, and Edge Locations and why they matter for performance and resilience.
In this lesson
Map infrastructure to design choices

Learn when to use Regions/AZs for availability, and Edge Locations for fast delivery and security at the edge.

Coming up
Edge caching layers

See how CloudFront PoPs and Regional Edge Caches reduce origin load and latency.

Practical
CLI exploration

Use a short CLI walkthrough to list Regions and AZs and relate them to edge coverage.

Explore Key Topics
Regions & AZs
Independent geographic clusters for core services and fault isolation.
Edge Locations
PoPs that cache and terminate connections close to users to reduce latency.
Edge Services
CloudFront, Global Accelerator, and WAF harness the edge for speed and security.
Visual overview
Regions
Global geographic clusters holding AZs and core services.
Availability Zones
Isolated data centers inside a region for high availability.
Edge Locations
Small PoPs and Regional Edge Caches placed close to users.
Key Takeaway

Design with user geography first: Regions for compute and resilience, Edge for low-latency delivery and security.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will develop four concrete capabilities that matter when designing global systems. First, you will be able to explain Regions, Availability Zones, and Edge Locations by name and function, so you can justify placement of services for resilience and locality. Second, you will learn to differentiate the roles of Regions/AZs versus Edge Locations — which layer is responsible for compute and state, and which layer is responsible for connection termination and caching. Third, you will understand the strategic importance of Edge Locations for latency reduction and cost control, including a clear mental model of when caching is appropriate. Fourth, you will identify edge services like CloudFront, Regional Edge Caches, Global Accelerator, and WAF and describe their primary functions. Each objective is designed so you can make a practical architecture decision: choose where to host origin servers, decide what to cache at the edge, and know how edge services improve both performance and security. As you work through the lessons, keep these goals in mind and test yourself with the reflection questions.

VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
Common pitfalls
Avoid caching highly dynamic or personalized responses at the PoP without proper headers, expiration, or invalidation. Edge caching is powerful, but must match content semantics.
Example: Cache product thumbnails at the PoP but keep checkout sessions in regional servers across AZs.
Tip: Use CloudFront behaviors and header controls to separate cacheable assets from dynamic endpoints.

screens.title: AWS Regions and Availability Zones
screens.narratorSegment: Regions and Availability Zones form the backbone of AWS's fault-tolerant architecture. A Region is a geographic area containing multiple Availability Zones, each of which is one or more discrete data centers with redundant power, networking, and connectivity. The key design idea is separation: AZs are physically separated by meaningful distances so that a localized failure, like a building-level power outage or flood, does not impact other AZs in the same Region. At the same time, AZs are close enough to provide low-latency network links for synchronous replication, multi-AZ databases, and cross-AZ load balancing. For example, you would place your primary database in one AZ and a replicated instance in another AZ within the same Region to survive a single datacenter failure. A common misconception is to treat AZs as single servers or racks; they are entire facilities with independent utility feeds and network uplinks. Another mistake is choosing a Region solely on cost; choose a Region that balances latency to your users, available services, and compliance requirements. Takeaway: use Regions for geographic presence and AZs for availability, and design your failover so that losing one AZ does not take your application offline. How would you partition stateful and stateless components across AZs to minimize recovery time?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Regions are isolated geographic clusters; AZs are independent data centers inside Regions for fault-tolerance and low-latency replication.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Regions & Availability Zones
Definition

A Region is a geographic area containing multiple AZs. An AZ is one or more discrete data centers with redundant systems and independent failure domains.

Why it matters
  • AZ separation preserves availability during localized failures.
  • Close AZs enable low-latency replication and synchronous services.
  • Regions provide fault isolation and data residency control.
Key Takeaway: Place stateful systems across AZs and pick Regions that balance latency, compliance, and service availability.
Concrete example — multi-AZ database
Host the primary database in AZ-A and a synchronous standby in AZ-B within the same Region. Use cross-AZ replication and load balancing for stateless application servers to survive a single AZ failure without data loss.
Misconception
AZs are not identical to Regions. You cannot assume AZs are immune to regional disasters, so critical resilience requires cross-region planning for extreme events.
Pro tip
Design stateless services to scale across AZs and put durable state in multi-AZ services or across Regions when required for disaster recovery.

screens.title: Edge Locations and Their Purpose
screens.narratorSegment: Edge Locations are smaller facilities placed near major population centers to serve user requests faster than a distant Region. Their principal function is to cache static content and to terminate user connections, so the first network hop is short. When a user requests an image or a script, that request is routed to the nearest Edge Location, which can serve the content from a cached copy. If the content is not cached in that local PoP, the request can be forwarded to a Regional Edge Cache or to the origin in a Region. This layered approach reduces round trips to the origin, decreases perceived latency for users, and reduces origin load and egress costs. A concrete example: a customer in London requests a product image; a London PoP served the image from cache in milliseconds rather than fetching it from a Region located hundreds of miles away. A common misunderstanding is to assume edge locations replace Regions for durable storage — they are cache and termination points only, not substitutes for origin storage or compute. The design decision you must make is which assets are safe and beneficial to cache at the edge versus which must remain served from the origin.

keyIdea.title: Edge role
keyIdea.text: Edge Locations shorten the user network path by caching content and terminating connections, improving latency and offloading origin servers.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Edge Locations
What an Edge Location does
  • Terminate client connections close to the user.
  • Cache static and semi-static content for immediate delivery.
  • Forward cache misses to Regional Edge Caches or origin Regions over the AWS backbone.
Analogy: Edge Locations are like local post offices that hold common parcels for quick pickup instead of sending every request back to a central warehouse.
Scenario

A user in Tokyo loads a video thumbnail. The nearest PoP serves it instantly. If the PoP doesn't have it, the request goes to a Regional Edge Cache which often has a larger copy, reducing trips back to the origin Region.

Misconception
Edge Locations are not full Regions and should not be used for persistent compute or primary storage assumptions.
Key Takeaway: Use PoPs for frequently accessed static assets and connection termination to achieve the fastest user experience.

screens.title: CloudFront PoPs vs Regional Edge Caches
screens.narratorSegment: AWS uses a two-tier caching strategy to maximize performance while managing cache capacity. The first tier is CloudFront Points of Presence, numerous small PoPs located in many cities. PoPs are optimized for proximity and minimal latency; they cache the most frequently requested objects. The second tier is Regional Edge Caches, which are larger and sit between PoPs and the origin. When a PoP does not have an object, it queries the Regional Edge Cache before going all the way to the origin. This reduces repeated origin fetches for less popular items and improves hit ratios across a region. A concrete example: very popular static assets are likely in every PoP, while less-frequently accessed images may only be retained in a nearby Regional Edge Cache, which still beats a full origin fetch. A common mistake is to assume every object will be present at every PoP. Instead, design your caching policy with an understanding of TTLs, object popularity, and cache capacity. The takeaway is simple: PoPs give speed, Regional Edge Caches add capacity and reduce origin load. How would you set TTLs and caching headers for product thumbnails versus personalized cart pages?

keyIdea.title: Two-tier caching
keyIdea.text: PoPs prioritize proximity and speed; Regional Edge Caches provide larger cache capacity and reduce origin fetches for less-frequent items.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › PoPs vs Regional Edge Caches
CloudFront Points of Presence
  • Many, widely distributed, optimized for lowest latency.
  • Smaller cache capacity; store hottest objects.
  • Best for frequently requested static assets.
Example: Homepage images that get millions of hits are likely present at most PoPs.
Regional Edge Caches
  • Fewer, larger caches between PoPs and origin.
  • Hold larger, less-frequently accessed objects.
  • Reduce origin requests for cache misses across multiple PoPs.
Key Takeaway: Use PoPs for speed and Regional Edge Caches for capacity to minimize origin load.
Pro tip
Tune TTLs: high request rate objects get longer TTLs; low-rate items rely on Regional Edge Caches.
Misconception
Do not expect every PoP to have every object; cache strategies matter.
Check
Measure cache-hit ratios and origin request rates to validate your policy.

screens.title: Edge Services: Global Accelerator and WAF
screens.narratorSegment: Edge infrastructure benefits more than just static web assets. AWS Global Accelerator and AWS WAF use Edge Locations to improve performance and security. Global Accelerator accepts traffic at the nearest Edge Location and sends it through the AWS global network backbone to your application endpoint. This optimizes network paths and is especially useful for non-HTTP traffic such as gaming or VoIP where latency and jitter matter. AWS WAF, when deployed with CloudFront or other edge-enabled endpoints, evaluates and filters requests at the edge before they reach your origin, reducing malicious traffic and protecting resources from common attacks. An example: a multiplayer game can use Global Accelerator to reduce round-trip times for UDP packets by entering the AWS backbone at the nearest PoP, while WAF blocks malicious HTTP requests at the PoP, avoiding extra load on regional servers. A common error is relying solely on DNS routing for performance; DNS doesn't optimize the network path the way Global Accelerator does. Key takeaway: leverage edge-based networking and filtering when low latency or early security enforcement materially improves user experience. Edge Services: Global Accelerator and WAF means global accelerator optimizes network paths for latency-sensitive traffic; waf enforces security at the edge to protect origins.. In practical terms, how non-http and security services take advantage of the edge. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Edge-enabled services
keyIdea.text: Global Accelerator optimizes network paths for latency-sensitive traffic; WAF enforces security at the edge to protect origins.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Global Accelerator & WAF
AWS Global Accelerator

Routes traffic through the AWS backbone from the nearest Edge Location to your application endpoint, improving performance for non-HTTP and latency-sensitive workloads.

Example: Multiplayer gaming traffic benefits from reduced jitter and fewer public internet hops when using Global Accelerator.
AWS WAF at the Edge

Filter malicious traffic at the edge to stop attacks before they consume origin resources, helpful for DDoS mitigation and common web exploits.

Key Takeaway: Use Global Accelerator for path optimization and WAF at the edge to prevent harmful traffic from reaching your origin.
Misconception
DNS geolocation does not ensure the best network path; Global Accelerator provides optimized routing through AWS network backbone.
Pro tip
Combine WAF with CloudFront to block bad traffic at the PoP and reduce origin costs.
Check
Measure latency and origin request volume before and after enabling edge services to validate benefit.

screens.title: Request Flow: From User to Origin
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the request flow helps you reason about latency, cache hits, and origin load. When a user makes a request, DNS and network routing send that request to the nearest CloudFront Point of Presence. If the requested content is cached there, the PoP serves it immediately. If not, the PoP checks the Regional Edge Cache to see if a larger, nearby cache holds the object. If the Regional Edge Cache also misses, the request traverses the AWS backbone to the origin in the appropriate Region, where the object is fetched and then cached on the return path. This layered process minimizes trips to the origin and concentrates origin fetches to fewer, larger caches. A concrete example: a user requests a video segment; the PoP serves it when cached. If the PoP misses but the Regional Edge Cache has it, the user still benefits from much lower latency than an origin fetch. Misconception: cache misses always mean high latency — with regional caching and the backbone, many misses are handled efficiently. Reflect: how would you design TTLs so frequently changing but still commonly requested content stays consistent without overloading the origin?

keyIdea.title: Request path
keyIdea.text: Requests go PoP → Regional Edge Cache → Origin; each tier reduces origin load and improves perceived latency.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Request Flow
Process: User request to origin
PoP → Regional Edge Cache → Origin over AWS backbone
Step cards
1. User request arrives at nearest PoP. Fastest possible first hop.
2. PoP checks local cache; serve on hit.
3. On miss, PoP queries Regional Edge Cache; larger capacity reduces origin fetches.
4. If still a miss, fetch from origin in a Region over the AWS backbone.
Example scenario

A web API returns a cacheable JSON file. If popular, PoPs store it. If less popular, the Regional Edge Cache keeps it so multiple PoPs avoid reaching the origin.

Key Takeaway: Each cache layer reduces origin load and improves response times for a broad set of requests.
Check your understanding
If your origin experiences unexpected spikes, inspect PoP and Regional Edge Cache hit rates before scaling origin capacity; a tuning of TTLs and cache behaviors often resolves the issue.

screens.title: Hands-on: Listing Regions and Availability Zones (CLI)
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough explains commands you can run to discover Regions and Availability Zones, so you can validate where to deploy. Use the EC2 describe-regions command to list Regions. The command returns region identifiers you can reference in infrastructure scripts. Next, select a specific Region and run describe-availability-zones with that Region to see the AZ names available there. This verification helps you ensure your chosen Region supports the services you require and lets you plan AZ-aware deployments. A concrete example: list Regions, pick us-east-1, and then list its AZs to confirm there are three or more AZs for a multi-AZ database deployment. A common mistake is assuming the same AZ names exist across all accounts; AZ name mappings can vary by account, so always query the target account. After running the commands, reflect: does the Region you picked balance user latency, required services, and compliance constraints? If not, repeat the discovery process for an alternate Region. Hands-on: Listing Regions and Availability Zones (CLI) means use aws ec2 describe-regions and describe-availability-zones to confirm available regions and azs before deploying.. In practical terms, verify available regions and azs using the aws cli. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › CLI: Regions & AZs
Commands to run
aws ec2 describe-regions --query 'Regions[].RegionName' --output text

aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --region us-east-1 --query 'AvailabilityZones[].ZoneName' --output text
These commands list Region names and AZ names so you can confirm deployment targets and script automation using accurate identifiers.
Concrete example

Run the first command to see available Regions. Choose one that has the services you need. Then run the second command with that Region to enumerate its AZs and use those AZ names in multi-AZ templates.

Misconception: AZ labels can map differently per account; always query the account you're operating in rather than assuming AZ names are globally identical.
Key Takeaway: Validating Regions and AZs via CLI avoids surprises during deployment and ensures your architecture's availability assumptions are grounded.

screens.title: Designing for Performance and Resilience
screens.narratorSegment: When you design global applications, map components to the infrastructure tiers based on durability, latency needs, and cost. Put durable, stateful systems like primary databases in Regions and replicate across multiple AZs for high availability. Deploy stateless application servers across AZs behind a load balancer so traffic can fail over smoothly. Place static assets, media, and downloadable scripts in S3 and serve them through CloudFront to leverage PoPs and Regional Edge Caches for fast delivery. For latency-sensitive non-HTTP traffic, consider Global Accelerator to route traffic via the AWS backbone from the closest Edge Location. Also use WAF at the edge to block malicious requests before they reach origin servers. A common error is overusing edge caching for dynamic content; ensure cacheability by designating clear TTLs and cache keys. Example partition: user sessions and cart state remain in Region-backed stores, while product images and static front-end bundles are cached at PoPs. Final question: which parts of your application can you safely offload to the edge without sacrificing correctness? Designing for Performance and Resilience means stateful services live in regions/azs; static and latency-sensitive traffic is pushed to edge services to improve user-perceived performance and reduce origin costs.. fullNarratorScript:
Today we begin with the physical foundation that underpins cloud reliability and speed. You will learn what Regions, Availability Zones, and Edge Locations are, why AWS separates them, and how that separation helps you design resilient, low-latency systems. Think of Regions as independent geographic clusters, Availability Zones as separate data centers inside a Region that share an AWS backbone, and Edge Locations as compact points of presence placed close to users for fast content delivery. We will also cover the two-tiered caching strategy used by CloudFront — local Points of Presence and larger Regional Edge Caches — plus how services like Global Accelerator and WAF use edge infrastructure to improve performance and security. By the end of this chapter you'll know which infrastructure component to choose for static assets, dynamic compute, or latency-sensitive traffic, and you'll be able to spot a common mistake: treating edge services as optional rather than strategic. As we move forward, think about your users’ geography and the nature of your content — those two facts drive the best architecture choices.

In this chapter you will develop four concrete capabilities that matter when designing global systems. First, you will be able to explain Regions, Availability Zones, and Edge Locations by name and function, so you can justify placement of services for resilience and locality. Second, you will learn to differentiate the roles of Regions/AZs versus Edge Locations — which layer is responsible for compute and state, and which layer is responsible for connection termination and caching. Third, you will understand the strategic importance of Edge Locations for latency reduction and cost control, including a clear mental model of when caching is appropriate. Fourth, you will identify edge services like CloudFront, Regional Edge Caches, Global Accelerator, and WAF and describe their primary functions. Each objective is designed so you can make a practical architecture decision: choose where to host origin servers, decide what to cache at the edge, and know how edge services improve both performance and security. As you work through the lessons, keep these goals in mind and test yourself with the reflection questions.

This second objectives slide focuses on application and verification. You will practice listing Regions and Availability Zones using the console and AWS CLI so you can confirm deployed services are in the intended locations. You will also explore CloudFront's distribution model and infer the presence of Edge Locations and Regional Edge Caches so you can reason about cache hit ratios and origin offload. The hands-on activity will ask you to compare the distribution of Regions and Edge Locations against your user base, to identify latency-sensitive endpoints, and to craft simple caching policies for static content. Why does this matter? Because a correct mapping reduces data transfer costs, improves response times, and prevents origin overload during traffic spikes. As you work, avoid a common mistake: caching dynamic, user-specific data at the PoP without appropriate invalidation and controls. That error leads to stale content being served to users. Finish by reflecting: which assets in your application are stable enough to cache at the edge, and which must stay in the origin?

Regions and Availability Zones form the backbone of AWS's fault-tolerant architecture. A Region is a geographic area containing multiple Availability Zones, each of which is one or more discrete data centers with redundant power, networking, and connectivity. The key design idea is separation: AZs are physically separated by meaningful distances so that a localized failure, like a building-level power outage or flood, does not impact other AZs in the same Region. At the same time, AZs are close enough to provide low-latency network links for synchronous replication, multi-AZ databases, and cross-AZ load balancing. For example, you would place your primary database in one AZ and a replicated instance in another AZ within the same Region to survive a single datacenter failure. A common misconception is to treat AZs as single servers or racks; they are entire facilities with independent utility feeds and network uplinks. Another mistake is choosing a Region solely on cost; choose a Region that balances latency to your users, available services, and compliance requirements. Takeaway: use Regions for geographic presence and AZs for availability, and design your failover so that losing one AZ does not take your application offline. How would you partition stateful and stateless components across AZs to minimize recovery time?

Edge Locations are smaller facilities placed near major population centers to serve user requests faster than a distant Region. Their principal function is to cache static content and to terminate user connections, so the first network hop is short. When a user requests an image or a script, that request is routed to the nearest Edge Location, which can serve the content from a cached copy. If the content is not cached in that local PoP, the request can be forwarded to a Regional Edge Cache or to the origin in a Region. This layered approach reduces round trips to the origin, decreases perceived latency for users, and reduces origin load and egress costs. A concrete example: a customer in London requests a product image; a London PoP served the image from cache in milliseconds rather than fetching it from a Region located hundreds of miles away. A common misunderstanding is to assume edge locations replace Regions for durable storage — they are cache and termination points only, not substitutes for origin storage or compute. The design decision you must make is which assets are safe and beneficial to cache at the edge versus which must remain served from the origin.

AWS uses a two-tier caching strategy to maximize performance while managing cache capacity. The first tier is CloudFront Points of Presence, numerous small PoPs located in many cities. PoPs are optimized for proximity and minimal latency; they cache the most frequently requested objects. The second tier is Regional Edge Caches, which are larger and sit between PoPs and the origin. When a PoP does not have an object, it queries the Regional Edge Cache before going all the way to the origin. This reduces repeated origin fetches for less popular items and improves hit ratios across a region. A concrete example: very popular static assets are likely in every PoP, while less-frequently accessed images may only be retained in a nearby Regional Edge Cache, which still beats a full origin fetch. A common mistake is to assume every object will be present at every PoP. Instead, design your caching policy with an understanding of TTLs, object popularity, and cache capacity. The takeaway is simple: PoPs give speed, Regional Edge Caches add capacity and reduce origin load. How would you set TTLs and caching headers for product thumbnails versus personalized cart pages?

Edge infrastructure benefits more than just static web assets. AWS Global Accelerator and AWS WAF use Edge Locations to improve performance and security. Global Accelerator accepts traffic at the nearest Edge Location and sends it through the AWS global network backbone to your application endpoint. This optimizes network paths and is especially useful for non-HTTP traffic such as gaming or VoIP where latency and jitter matter. AWS WAF, when deployed with CloudFront or other edge-enabled endpoints, evaluates and filters requests at the edge before they reach your origin, reducing malicious traffic and protecting resources from common attacks. An example: a multiplayer game can use Global Accelerator to reduce round-trip times for UDP packets by entering the AWS backbone at the nearest PoP, while WAF blocks malicious HTTP requests at the PoP, avoiding extra load on regional servers. A common error is relying solely on DNS routing for performance; DNS doesn't optimize the network path the way Global Accelerator does. Key takeaway: leverage edge-based networking and filtering when low latency or early security enforcement materially improves user experience. Edge Services: Global Accelerator and WAF means global accelerator optimizes network paths for latency-sensitive traffic; waf enforces security at the edge to protect origins.. In practical terms, how non-http and security services take advantage of the edge. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding the request flow helps you reason about latency, cache hits, and origin load. When a user makes a request, DNS and network routing send that request to the nearest CloudFront Point of Presence. If the requested content is cached there, the PoP serves it immediately. If not, the PoP checks the Regional Edge Cache to see if a larger, nearby cache holds the object. If the Regional Edge Cache also misses, the request traverses the AWS backbone to the origin in the appropriate Region, where the object is fetched and then cached on the return path. This layered process minimizes trips to the origin and concentrates origin fetches to fewer, larger caches. A concrete example: a user requests a video segment; the PoP serves it when cached. If the PoP misses but the Regional Edge Cache has it, the user still benefits from much lower latency than an origin fetch. Misconception: cache misses always mean high latency — with regional caching and the backbone, many misses are handled efficiently. Reflect: how would you design TTLs so frequently changing but still commonly requested content stays consistent without overloading the origin?

A common mistake is assuming the same AZ names exist across all accounts; AZ name mappings can vary by account, so always query the target account. After running the commands, reflect: does the Region you picked balance user latency, required services, and compliance constraints? If not, repeat the discovery process for an alternate Region.
